result:
The dirt trails that appear where people ignore the sidewalk have a name: desire paths. You've seen them: a diagonal scar across a campus lawn, a shortcut worn through a hedge near a bus stop. It's a lovelier name than a strip of dead grass seems to deserve.

I like them because they're a record of disagreement. Someone drew a right angle, and thousands of feet voted for the hypotenuse. No one organized it. Each person just walked where walking made sense, and the grass kept the tally.

Some designers have learned to listen. There's a story, told about several universities and probably true of at least one, that the builders laid no walkways at first. They waited a year, watched where the grass died, and paved those lines. In Finland, planners reportedly visit parks after fresh snowfall to see which routes the footprints trace.

What strikes me is how rare this patience is. Most things get built from a guess about how people will behave, and then the guess is defended. The fence goes up across the shortcut. A sign appears. The path reappears a meter to the left.

The same thing happens outside landscaping. Language has desire paths: singular "they" was trampled into the lawn for centuries before the style guides paved it. Software has them too, in every workaround users invent for a feature nobody thought to build.

A worn trail is cheap, honest information about what people want. Usually the best response is to fetch the gravel.
